sources.entry: Stop Avoiding Politics is a good contrarian take on the current (negative) connotation of the word "politics".

summary.title: Stop Avoiding Politics
summary.one_liner: Workplace politics is how people coordinate influence in any organization, and refusing to engage with it lets bad decisions win by default; engineers should learn to practice "good politics."
takeaways: Politics is the informal network of relationships and influence present in every organization; refusing to take part does not remove it.
Bad technical decisions often happen because people with the right information were absent from the room.
Good politics means building relationships early, understanding real incentives, managing up, creating win-win outcomes, and being visible.
The same skills can be used to manipulate or to get good ideas implemented; the difference is how they are used.
summary.summary: The author, a former engineer who once disdained workplace politics, argues that politics is simply how humans coordinate influence in groups and that avoiding it means decisions get made without you. The essay uses examples of poor technical decisions to show how well-connected people win debates even when their ideas are worse. It then lists practical habits of "good politics": building relationships before you need them, framing proposals around stakeholder incentives, managing up, seeking win-win deals, and making your work visible. It is a short opinion piece with no code or tooling.
